cards.title: Anthropic is burning gas to feed the AI boom
cards.title_cn: Anthropic 正在燃烧天然气来推动人工智能的繁荣
cards.summary: 【Anthropic】As it prepares to go public, Anthropic's S-1 filing makes generative AI's methane dependency glaringly obvious. "Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate pow…
fulltext: Anthropic is clear that data centers will run on gas, to the company’s own detriment.
As it prepares to go public, Anthropic’s S-1 filing makes generative AI’s methane dependency glaringly obvious.
“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense.”

In documents filed with the US Securities and Exchange Commission Monday, Anthropic acknowledges that data centers are becoming increasingly reliant on “natural gas” — the fossil fuel industry’s marketing term for what is primarily methane — leaving the company’s AI data center buildout vulnerable to rising fuel costs and existing supply chain constraints. And in a possible catch-22, Anthropic admits that rising global temperatures — a symptom of burning fossil fuels — will increase the company’s operating costs.

“Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,” Anthropic says, adding that some of its planned data centers rely on electricity generated by natural gas turbines on-site. Anthropic leases capacity from hyperscalers, but it announced a $50 billion dollar plan last year to expand data centers in Texas and New York.

The US, the epicenter for data centers globally, is planning to build more fossil fuel generation capacity than it has in a decade as data centers demand more electricity. Donald Trump’s administration has sought to kill renewable energy projects while tilting the regulatory landscape in favor of fossil fuels, which Trump claims is a more important energy source for powering data centers around the clock than solar and wind farms that generate power intermittently.

Now, a shortage of gas turbines is slowing data center construction. Some developers are installing gas engines on-site as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to power grids. Developers are also turning to more simple turbine technology at these sites as they face backlogs from turbine manufacturers, making on-site power generation less efficient and more polluting as a result.

Data center electricity demand could wipe out decades of gains in air quality over the next five years, one recent Texas-based study found — raising levels of soot, smog-forming pollutants, and planet-heating carbon dioxide. Even as data centers create more greenhouse gas pollution, Anthropic’s S-1 points to climate change as a risk to its bottom line. It will have to pay more for electricity and water to cool servers at data centers as temperatures climb.

Nevertheless, Anthropic expects increased competition for natural gas and pipeline capacity from hyperscalers and cloud service providers rushing to build their own data centers. “This competition could drive up the price of natural gas,” the company notes.

Gas makes up the biggest chunk of the US electricity mix, 40 percent of the nation’s power generation. And Americans are already feeling the pain of rising costs as utilities scramble to upgrade energy infrastructure and meet rising power demand.

Pissed-off residents have successfully blocked dozens of proposed data centers across the US. Anthropic acknowledges that the specter of ballooning utility bills is enough to interfere with a data center project. “If our efforts to secure electrical power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions, standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts,” it says.

If regulators push data center developers to shoulder more of the costs for new energy infrastructure, Anthropic says that could also raise its operating costs. And without a secure gas supply and the pipelines to transport the fuel, the company says, it might need to delay or abandon planned data center projects altogether.
Ultimately, these challenges could stunt Anthropic’s growth:

Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers.

cards.summary_cn: 【Anthropic】在准备上市之际，Anthropic 的 S-1 文件让生成型人工智能对甲烷的依赖变得显而易见。 “争夺拥有充足电力的电力供应和数据中心位置的竞争......
fulltext_cn: Anthropic 明确表示，数据中心将依靠天然气运行，这对公司自身不利。
在准备上市之际，Anthropic 的 S-1 文件让生成型人工智能对甲烷的依赖变得显而易见。
“对于获得充足电力供应和数据中心位置的竞争非常激烈。”
在周一向美国证券交易委员会提交的文件中，Anthropic 承认数据中心越来越依赖“天然气”（化石燃料行业的营销术语，主要是甲烷），这使得该公司的人工智能数据中心建设很容易受到燃料成本上涨和现有供应链限制的影响。在可能的第 22 条军规中，Anthropic 承认全球气温上升（燃烧化石燃料的一个症状）将增加公司的运营成本。
Anthropic 表示：“对电力供应和具有充足电力供应的数据中心位置的竞争非常激烈。”他补充说，其计划中的一些数据中心依赖于现场天然气涡轮机产生的电力。 Anthropic 从超大规模企业租赁容量，但它去年宣布了一项 500 亿美元的计划，用于扩建德克萨斯州和纽约的数据中心。
作为全球数据中心的中心，美国正计划建设比十年来更多的化石燃料发电能力，因为数据中心需要更多的电力。唐纳德·特朗普政府试图扼杀可再生能源项目，同时将监管环境向有利于化石燃料的方向倾斜，特朗普声称，与间歇性发电的太阳能和风电场相比，化石燃料是全天候为数据中心供电的更重要的能源。
现在，燃气轮机的短缺正在减缓数据中心的建设。一些开发商正在现场安装燃气发动机，以避免连接电网的漫长等待时间。由于面临涡轮机制造商的积压，开发商也在这些地点转向更简单的涡轮机技术，从而导致现场发电效率降低、污染加剧。
德克萨斯州最近的一项研究发现，数据中心的电力需求可能会抹去未来五年空气质量几十年来的进步——导致烟尘、烟雾形成污染物和地球加热二氧化碳的水平上升。尽管数据中心造成了更多的温室气体污染，Anthropic 的 S-1 仍指出气候变化对其盈利构成风险。随着气温上升，它将不得不支付更多的电费和水费来冷却数据中心的服务器。
尽管如此，Anthropic 预计超大型企业和云服务提供商争相建设自己的数据中心，对天然气和管道容量的竞争将加剧。该公司指出：“这种竞争可能会推高天然气价格。”
天然气占美国电力结构的最大部分，占全国发电量的 40%。随着公用事业公司争相升级能源基础设施并满足不断增长的电力需求，美国人已经感受到成本上涨的痛苦。
愤怒的居民已经成功封锁了美国各地数十个拟议的数据中心。 Anthropic 承认，不断膨胀的水电费足以干扰数据中心项目。报告称：“如果我们确保电力安全的努力被认为会影响其他公用事业客户和更广泛的电网，监管机构可能会施加条件、备用费用或旨在解决此类影响的其他要求。”
Anthropic 表示，如果监管机构迫使数据中心开发商承担更多新能源基础设施的成本，这也可能会提高其运营成本。该公司表示，如果没有安全的天然气供应和运输燃料的管道，它可能需要推迟或完全放弃计划中的数据中心项目。
最终，这些挑战可能会阻碍 Anthropic 的发展：
任何未能确保获得足够电力的行为、任何限制电力供应的法律、监管或其他行政行为或变化，或者能源或合规成本的任何显着增加，都可能对我们的成本结构产生不利影响，并限制我们扩展计算基础设施、开发和部署模型以及服务客户的能力。

cards.title: Kevin Roose is AGI-pilled. Why aren’t you?
cards.title_cn: 凯文·罗斯 (Kevin Roose) 充满了 AGI。你为什么不呢？
cards.summary: 【The Verge】Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry. Kevin was a longtime New York Tim…
fulltext: The author of The AGI Chronicles and co-host of Machine Gods on going all-in on YouTube and the AI race.
Today, I’m talking to Kevin Roose, journalist and author of the new book The AGI Chronicles, which details the recent and explosive transformation of the AI industry.

Kevin was a longtime New York Times reporter and host of the popular podcast Hard Fork, but he and friend of the show Casey Newton just left the Times to start the all-new tech podcast Machine Gods, which launched last week.

Kevin and I talked about launching Machine Gods and what it’s like to go from The New York Times to being an independent creator — and then of course we talked about the book, which is an excellently reported dive into the companies racing to build artificial general intelligence.

I wanted to get a sense from Kevin of what it was like to report this, to try and understand these characters and this moment in time, and where it all goes next. Fair warning: This conversation takes a pretty philosophical turn at the end, but I think you’ll find it a really worthwhile back-and-forth.
Okay: Kevin Roose on The AGI Chronicles, starting Machine Gods, and where AI goes from here. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Kevin Roose, you are the author of The AGI Chronicles and the cofounder and cohost of the new podcast Machine Gods. Welcome to Decoder.
Thanks so much for having me.
I was listening to the first episode of Machine Gods and you and Casey discussed the fact that technically you have the title of CEO.

It’s true. I won the coin flip and we needed someone. When you start a company as we have, you need to list someone as the CEO, I guess, to know who to haul in front of Congress when our first scandal inevitably breaks. So that’s going to be me.
It’s funny because you’re a CEO on Decoder. It means I’m going to have to ask you the Decoder questions.
[Laughs] Okay. Well, I’ve been a CEO for about five minutes and most days I frankly forget I’m the CEO.
Honestly, that tracks with most of the CEOs on the show. They all act like they’ve only done it for five minutes. We’ll come to it.

I want to talk about your book. It’s called The AGI Chronicles. It is a meticulously reported book about the main frontier labs and the culture shift they’ve all undergone as AI has come into the forefront and become a much more commercial product in many ways.

But let’s just start with Machine Gods. You were a journalist for The New York Times for a long time. Obviously, I think the audience probably knows this, but you and I have known each other for a long time. I will say that since I have known you, your desire to be a YouTuber has been top of mind. You’re just like, “How do I get over there?” And I’ve always been like, “Run, don’t do it.” But you did it.

You left The Times, you started your own podcast with our friend Casey Newton. It is the next generation of the very popular podcast, Hard Fork, which was excellent. And I’m excited for you, but what made you take the leap?
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
Yeah, you have been trying to convince me out of this for as long as I’ve been trying to convince myself into it and you have not succeeded because here I am.
Yep, I failed. Utterly failed.

No, look, I think that for some very good reasons, media companies have long been a little bit wary of going all in on YouTube or any other video platform. The ones that have gone all in have not necessarily come out of that with good feelings about it because there are a lot of–
Yeah, they pivot to video and also into death, routinely.

Yeah, you pivot to video or you sort of waste a bunch of money doing things that don’t pay for themselves. So, I think there are some structural economic reasons for that, but I also think it’s that there aren’t a lot of institutions that are equipped to make that kind of a long-term bet.

I’ve been trying to YouTube-pill people in media for many years, as you know. You’ve been trying to undo the YouTube-pilling on your end, but I just think it’s clearly the most important media platform in the world right now. It’s a place where journalism has not historically had a central place.

If you were to look at YouTube as a whole and try to assess what piece of it is dedicated to what you or I would consider high-quality journalism, it’s a vanishingly small part of the overall ecosystem there.

So, part of my mission is just to crack that and figure out how to do YouTube and video in general in a way that is sustainable from an economic and a sort of creative standpoint. And then just to experiment and do a bunch of things.

This is not a face that needs to be on YouTube. So I’m also hoping to bring some other people in and nail some formats. But I look at what The Verge has done there. I look at what people like Joanna Stern and MKBHD have done there. To me, that is very exciting and it’s a space where there’s a lot less competition than text or podcasts.
Machine Gods is a podcast that you’re doing in partnership with NPR, which I want to talk about. But do you think of it as a YouTube product?

We want it to be video-first. What that means basically is that we are going to give a shit about what it looks like to a degree that we have not always done. We’re going to try to give people a lot of reasons to want to watch as well as listen.

Obviously, we know that there are some people who just don’t like video podcasts and so we want to give the audio audience something that is enjoyable, but this is the direction of things. You can’t do a podcast now without doing video on top of it. So we’re going to try to really embrace that and make a good version of it that is as good as two middle-aged journalists can pull off on YouTube.
Truly the future of media is middle-aged journalists pivoting to YouTube. I feel the same way because I’m now making more video and that’s what we’re doing. It’s going to be great.

The other reason to leave and to do this — and obviously people know I’m friends with Casey as well, and I’ve been talking to you and him about it for a long time — is that the AI story is here. There is a platform shift. There are new companies, new characters, new ideas to talk about in the world. It’s funny because in that context, usually you get a media shift as well. The way we tell stories or the formats we tell stories usually shifts alongside the thing we are talking about or the technology we’re talking about.

Here, YouTube feels like the most solid media foundation that exists. It’s the one that’s the same the most, even though it’s changing and it has YouTube Shorts and now you can A / B test everything, including your own face. But it’s the one that is the most the same. Instagram has undergone some massive change and it feels like that will continue happening.
Does it feel like YouTube is the most stable place to build as you’re trying to tell these new stories?

It does. I mean, obviously you never want to put all your eggs in one basket. So, we are also distributing video on Apple Podcasts and Spotify and we’re going to be everywhere. But yeah, it feels relatively stable.

The question I’m always wondering is what would it take to replace YouTube? Many companies have tried to replace YouTube, but to do that, you would not only have to build an experience that was better for creators and better for users, but you would also have to replicate the entire visual corpus of humanity. You would have to just get 6 million videos from plumbers about how to fix every individual sink and then upload it to that. It’s a really hard thing to displace. It is so ingrained for so many people, and I just think it’s going to keep growing.

We’ll come to this when we talk about AI, but a long time ago I asked Google CEO Sundar Pichai, “Well, what are you going to do if there’s no more websites?” And he was kind of like, “Well, we have YouTube.” And there’s just no arguing with that. You sure do. And it is just going to keep growing.
What has been the most surprising thing about going from The New York Times to what you might call the creator economy?

Well, we’re very new at it, but surprising to me so far is how much I like all the business stuff. I think in journalism, you’re always taught to stay in your lane, and I have never run a business before. Casey has run a business. I knew he enjoyed it. But for me, these are new muscles and I don’t enjoy all of it. Negotiating the insurance quotes for our defamation coverage is not what I would feel compelled by. But regarding actually running a business, there is something to this founder thing.

Yeah, it’s a good time. It’s funny, in talking to you and to Casey and Joanna, who also just left and started her own thing, that comes up a lot. From my perspective, it’s why I’ve been doing this a long time. What if I stopped running the business? That doesn’t seem to be a choice. This is the future of media — taking control of your business and taking control of your audience. There’s something very powerful there.

One of the things I want to talk about, and then I definitely want to talk about the book at length, is the audience for AI coverage, because I see it in two ways. There’s a group of people building the stuff that loves it and wants to consume all of it. There’s a group of people that truly hates it and thinks all of it is fake.

And then there’s what I would call an expanding group in the middle where the products have become more useful. You have to look at them and evaluate them as they are. They were not terribly useful a couple years ago. The promises did not match reality, but every day now it can do one more thing that it couldn’t do before. Whether that thing is hacking all of the websites in the world, we’ll set that aside, but AI can do things it couldn’t do before and the audience seems to be changing.
How are you thinking about the audience for Machine Gods and how it might grow or change?

I mean, right now we’re just trying a bunch of stuff that we think will be good and we hope that it will find its sort of natural audience. But I think you’re right that the audience is changing. I think for a while there was a lot of demand for cope — basically people telling you this is not happening, you don’t have to pay attention to it, it sucks, it’s hurting the environment.

There still is in some parts of the internet. YouTube has a weird amount of this still going on and Reddit is also very anti-AI. But I think most people, or at least maybe a plurality of people, are either resigned to or excited about the fact that this is not going away. That is the audience that we’re looking for.

We’re not trying to tell you that AI is amazing and we’re going to be in AI utopia under the new machine regime. We’re also not telling you that this stuff is fake and sucks and is going to go away on its own and so we don’t need to do anything to regulate it or be worried about it. Casey’s phrase for this is AI realism. He thinks there’s a big chunk of people who are just sort of curious and interested and maybe a little scared, but their reaction to the fear is not to try to bury their heads in the sand, but to try to understand the thing.

So we started feeling this when we were doing Hard Fork where we would do something that just seemed kind of not our vibe. We would do a Claude Code walkthrough tutorial where we would just spend half an hour building a website and film ourselves and throw it up and it would do great. So people clearly were curious, and even if the comments on the videos were all from people who hated AI, there was clearly a lot of demand out there for people who were just like, “I kind of want to know what’s going on.”
“I hate that I can’t stop watching this” is a real theme inside of AI coverage for a variety of reasons.

Let’s talk about the book. I think that’s going to frame a bunch of the other questions I have. The book is meticulously reported. It is really fun to read. And the point of it, as I’ve heard you describe it, is to tell the history of the deep learning revolution because all these people just talk in Signal and in extremely childish tweets.

Tell me about that gap because this is an industry that is obsessed with documenting itself for computers and being legible to computers and not at all to other people, which seems wild to me. So explain the reporting of this book, because it feels like convincing them to even tell you what happened was a slog.

It was, yeah. So basically the reason I wrote this is because I was scared that all of this stuff was going to disappear. I am a history buff. I love to read books about the Wright brothers or the electrification of rural America or the moments of great invention during the PC revolution. I’m such a sucker for that stuff.

What you notice as you read more of these books is just that they all rely on a lot of contemporaneous notes and evidence — the lab notes from the scientists developing the atomic bomb, the correspondence between the Wright brothers and their friends and business partners — that is preserved and archived.

It was just clear to me reporting on AI every day that there was not going to be anything remotely similar for this stuff because A, all the people building this stuff work for private companies. They’re not government employees who are legally required to preserve their correspondence. And B, the Signal messages and Slack messages are all set by the lawyers to auto-delete after a certain period. So there was literally going to be kind of a mass disappearance with each passing year of these, I think, historically important artifacts, moments, and stories.

And then C, the researchers are all too busy to keep notes. They’re all grinding because they’re trying to build the machine god. So, I thought as a journalist, but more so almost as a historian, which is not a role I’ve ever officially played, but one I think I was playing with this book. I was just like, “I’ve got to just get this stuff because I have this sort of privileged ringside seat. These people talk to me. I know some of them will sit down and talk to me and tell me the stories.”

We did a lot of it on background so they could be protected from the consequences of talking to me. But this was sort of my attempt to furiously get all the stuff and put it in the archive where future generations could look at it.

The theme that really jumps out at me as I read the book was there’s a moment when AGI goes from being a thing they’re all dreaming about to being a thing that they all have to build and the shackles come off and they say, “We have to do this,” and they all drive toward it as hard as they can.

You talk specifically about Google where the Overton window moved and suddenly the people inside of Google, who thought this was all a pipe dream and pretty silly, started talking about AGI. That moment feels like the single most important moment in the history of AI, where “Won’t it be great?” goes to “We better go as fast as we can.”
Talk about that a little bit, because that shift inside these companies feels under-reported.

Yeah, I think that’s absolutely right. I mean, people have been talking and writing about AGI or some precursor that wasn’t called AGI but meant the same thing since literally antiquity. And especially since the 1950s, when the term artificial intelligence was born, people were talking about it. Alan Turing was writing about the thinking machine that could do anything the human brain could.

So this concept has been around for a long time, but there was no technology anywhere on the market or in research labs that could actually do what people wanted it to do — that could take in information, learn to learn about that information, and then use that to make predictions and act in the world. People tried lots of different ways to do this and none of them worked all that well.

What really needed to happen was the transformer needed to come along. This architecture that Google developed in 2017 and published and then presented to, among other places, OpenAI, which took the idea of the transformer and ran with it. And that’s the T in ChatGPT today. But that was the–
Somewhere a Google PR person just leapt out of a bush to hand you a check.
They do love this line.
They love it when you say it. They get so happy.
They love it. They love it less when you point out that although they invented it, they absolutely failed to turn it into a product until after OpenAI did.

But yeah, it was a dream, but there was nothing to attach to the dream. There was no technology. And then the large language model came and suddenly it was like, “Oh, maybe this is the thing that could scale forever and keep improving over many orders of magnitude.” So, that’s the light bulb that goes off at OpenAI and then later at Google is like, “Now we have the tool to do the thing that we have always wanted to do.”

You’ve got a line in there where you just point out that next-token prediction has not failed yet — that it is doing all the things people want it to do. We’ve obviously had to develop lots of technology around it. There are harnesses to make agents work. There’s reinforcement learning. There’s all this stuff around it. But that core technology has scaled.

The reason I bring that up is that in 2023 into 2024, I would ask every AI person who would come on the show or that we would see on The Verge whether LLMs can do it. Can they do the thing you want them to do? Because I don’t think at that moment it was clear that they could.

We’re closer now. They’re all openly talking about AGI. We are watching Meta’s Muse just walk its little butt around the internet whenever it wants. Do you think LLMs can do it? Do you think they can get there?

I think they can. I’m not certain about that, but they’ve been shockingly good and effective so far. If you go back and you look at the first LLMs, it’s just like 99 percent of people thought this is crazy, that this won’t scale. And then it just keeps working at every stage, at every order of magnitude. I’ve asked people, what was it about next-token prediction that was clearly superior to everything that came before it? There have been people who have told me this actually exists in the human brain too. There’s a whole school of thought that says that what is happening inside the human brain is essentially next-token prediction at scale. Obviously, it’s more complicated. These are not one-for-one replicas of each other.

But I think this is the fundamental mystery at the heart of AI: why is next-token prediction so remarkably effective? I think we don’t know. I kind of think it’s one of these cosmic mysteries, but why all of this works is because next-token prediction turns out to generalize really, really, really well.

There’s a part of that where all these companies had to believe it. Dario Amodei of Anthropic obviously wrote his paper, “Big Blob of Compute,” where he said you can just do it. You can just dump data and compute at this and we’ll get there. Everyone else had to be convinced of this.
What path did the AI companies all take to be convinced of this, and are they all fully convinced of it now?

I don’t think they’re all fully convinced of it now. I think they are convinced of it to varying degrees. Ilya Sutskever has this phrase, “Feel the AGI,” that he would walk floor to floor at OpenAI chanting in the old days and reminding people to feel the AGI. I think the labs feel the AGI to varying degrees. I think Anthropic is clearly the most AGI-pilled of the labs, with OpenAI kind of a close second.

And then there’s Google, which I think has always struggled to feel the AGI. I think there are lots of reasons for that, but it’s very funny. I love this section of the book where there’s this internal memo battle at Google, where they would just go on their internal message boards and Googlers love to write these manifestos and then snipe at each other’s manifestos and things like that.

fulltext_cn: 《The AGI Chronicles》的作者和《Machine Gods》的联合主持人谈如何全力投入 YouTube 和人工智能竞赛。
今天，我正在采访凯文·罗斯 (Kevin Roose)，他是记者兼新书《AGI 编年史》的作者，该书详细介绍了人工智能行业最近发生的爆炸性变革。
凯文是《纽约时报》的长期记者，也是热门播客《硬分叉》的主持人，但他和该节目的朋友凯西·牛顿刚刚离开《纽约时报》，开始上周推出的全新科技播客《机器之神》。
凯文和我讨论了《机器之神》的推出，以及从《纽约时报》成为一名独立创作者的感受——当然，我们还讨论了这本书，这本书对那些竞相构建通用人工智能的公司进行了精彩的报道。
我想从凯文那里了解报道此事的感受，尝试理解这些角色和此时此刻，以及接下来的发展。公平警告：这次谈话最后发生了相当哲学的转变，但我认为你会发现这是一次非常值得的来回。
好的：Kevin Roose 谈《AGI 编年史》、《机器之神》的启动以及人工智能的未来发展。开始了。
为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。
Kevin Roose，您是《AGI Chronicles》的作者，也是新播客 Machine Gods 的联合创始人和联合主持人。欢迎来到解码器。
非常感谢你邀请我。
我正在听《机器之神》的第一集，你和凯西讨论了这样一个事实：从技术上讲，你拥有首席执行官的头衔。
这是真的。我赢得了抛硬币，我们需要有人。我想，当你像我们一样创办一家公司时，你需要任命某人为首席执行官，以便知道当我们的第一起丑闻不可避免地爆发时该将谁带到国会面前。那就是我。
这很有趣，因为你是 Decoder 的首席执行官。这意味着我将不得不问你有关解码器的问题。
[笑]好的。好吧，我担任首席执行官大约五分钟，坦白说，大多数时候我都忘记了我是首席执行官。
老实说，这与节目中的大多数首席执行官都是一致的。他们都表现得好像只做了五分钟。我们会谈到它。
我想谈谈你的书。它的名字叫《AGI 编年史》。这是一本精心报道的书，介绍了主要的前沿实验室以及随着人工智能走入前沿并在许多方面成为更加商业化的产品，它们所经历的文化转变。
但让我们从机器之神开始吧。您曾长期担任《纽约时报》记者。显然，我想观众可能都知道这一点，但你和我已经认识很长时间了。我想说，自从我认识你以来，你想成为一名 YouTuber 的愿望就一直是你的首要任务。你就像，“我怎么去那里？”我总是说，“跑吧，别这么做。”但你做到了。
你离开了《泰晤士报》，和我们的朋友凯西·牛顿一起开始了自己的播客。它是非常流行的播客硬分叉的下一代，非常棒。我为你感到兴奋，但是是什么让你迈出了这一步呢？
Verge 订阅者，不要忘记，无论您在何处获取播客，都可以获得无广告解码器的独占访问权限。前往这里。还不是订阅者？您可以在这里注册。
是的，只要我一直试图说服自己，你就一直在试图说服我放弃这件事，但你没有成功，因为我在这里。
是的，我失败了。彻底失败了。
不，我认为出于一些非常好的原因，媒体公司长期以来对全力投入 YouTube 或任何其他视频平台持谨慎态度。那些全力以赴的人不一定会对此有良好的感觉，因为有很多——
是的，他们经常转向视频，也转向死亡。
是的，你转向视频，或者你浪费了一大笔钱去做一些无法收回成本的事情。所以，我认为这有一些结构性的经济原因，但我也认为没有很多机构有能力进行这种长期押注。
如你所知，多年来我一直在尝试在 YouTube 上对媒体界的人进行避孕。你们一直在努力消除 YouTube 的影响，但我认为它显然是目前世界上最重要的媒体平台。这是一个新闻业历史上并未占据中心地位的地方。
如果你将 YouTube 作为一个整体来看待，并尝试评估其中的哪一部分致力于你或我认为的高质量新闻，那么它只是整个生态系统中微不足道的一小部分。
因此，我的使命之一就是解决这个问题，并找出如何以一种从经济和创意角度来看可持续的方式来制作 YouTube 和视频。然后只是尝试并做很多事情。
这不是一张需要出现在 YouTube 上的面孔。因此，我也希望引入其他一些人并确定一些格式。但我看看 The Verge 在那里做了什么。我看看乔安娜·斯特恩 (Joanna Stern) 和 MKBHD 等人在那里做了什么。对我来说，这非常令人兴奋，而且这个领域的竞争比文本或播客要少得多。
《机器之神》是您与 NPR 合作制作的一个播客，我想谈谈它。但你认为它是 YouTube 产品吗？
我们希望它是视频优先的。这基本上意味着我们将在某种程度上关心它的样子，而我们并不总是这样做。我们将尽力为人们提供很多想要观看和聆听的理由。
显然，我们知道有些人不喜欢视频播客，因此我们想为音频观众提供一些令人愉快的东西，但这就是事情的方向。现在如果不制作视频就无法制作播客。因此，我们将尝试真正接受这一点，并制作一个好的版本，就像两名中年记者在 YouTube 上可以完成的那样。
真正媒体的未来是转向 YouTube 的中年记者。我也有同样的感觉，因为我现在正在制作更多视频，这就是我们正在做的事情。会很棒的。
离开并这样做的另一个原因——显然人们也知道我也是凯西的朋友，而且我已经和你和他谈论这件事很长时间了——是人工智能的故事就在这里。有一个平台转移。世界上有新公司、新人物、新想法可供谈论。这很有趣，因为在这种情况下，通常你也会发生媒体转变。我们讲故事的方式或讲故事的格式通常会随着我们正在谈论的事情或我们正在谈论的技术而变化。
在这里，YouTube 感觉像是现有的最坚实的媒体基础。它是最相同的一个，尽管它在变化，而且它有 YouTube Shorts，现在你可以对一切进行 A/B 测试，包括你自己的脸。但这是最相似的。 Instagram 已经发生了一些巨大的变化，而且这种变化似乎还会继续发生。
当您尝试讲述这些新故事时，您是否觉得 YouTube 是最稳定的构建场所？
确实如此。我的意思是，显然你永远不想把所有鸡蛋放在一个篮子里。因此，我们还在 Apple Podcasts 和 Spotify 上分发视频，我们将无处不在。但是，是的，感觉相对稳定。
我一直想知道如何才能取代 YouTube？许多公司都试图取代 YouTube，但要做到这一点，你不仅需要打造一种对创作者和用户都更好的体验，而且还必须复制人类的整个视觉语料库。您只需从水管工那里获取 600 万个关于如何修理每个水槽的视频，然后将其上传到该视频即可。这确实是一件很难取代的事情。它对很多人来说是如此根深蒂固，而且我认为它会继续增长。
当我们谈论人工智能时，我们会谈到这一点，但很久以前，我问谷歌首席执行官桑达尔·皮查伊（Sundar Pichai），“好吧，如果没有更多的网站，你会做什么？”他有点像，“好吧，我们有 YouTube。”这是毫无争议的。你一定会的。而且它只会继续增长。
从《纽约时报》转向所谓的创作者经济，最令人惊讶的事情是什么？
嗯，我们在这方面还很陌生，但到目前为止令我惊讶的是我是多么喜欢所有的商业东西。我认为在新闻行业，你总是被教导要走自己的路，而我以前从未经营过企业。凯西经营一家企业。我知道他很享受。但对我来说，这些都是新的肌肉，我并不喜欢这一切。我不会觉得有必要就诽谤保险的保险报价进行谈判。但就实际经营一家企业而言，这位创始人的事情是有道理的。
是的，这是一个好时机。有趣的是，在与你以及凯西和乔安娜交谈时，他们也刚刚离开并开始了自己的事业，这出现了很多。从我的角度来看，这就是我长期以来一直这样做的原因。如果我停止经营业务怎么办？这似乎不是一个选择。这就是媒体的未来——控制你的业务并控制你的受众。那里有一些非常强大的东西。
我想谈论的一件事，然后我肯定想详细谈论这本书，是人工智能报道的受众，因为我从两个方面看待它。有一群人在创造自己喜欢的东西，并且想要消费掉所有的东西。有一群人真的讨厌它，并认为所有这些都是假的。
然后是我所说的中间不断扩大的群体，产品变得更加有用。你必须观察它们并评估它们的本来面目。几年前它们还不是很有用。承诺与现实不符，但现在每天它都能多做一件以前做不到的事情。无论那件事是黑客攻击世界上所有的网站，我们都会把它放在一边，但人工智能可以做以前做不到的事情，而且受众似乎正在发生变化。
您如何看待《机器之神》的观众群体以及他们可能会如何增长或变化？
我的意思是，现在我们只是尝试一些我们认为好的东西，我们希望它能找到自然的受众。但我认为你说的对，观众正在发生变化。我认为有一段时间，人们对应对的需求很大——基本上人们告诉你这不会发生，你不必关注它，这很糟糕，它正在损害环境。
互联网的某些部分仍然存在。 YouTube 上仍然有大量这样的事情发生，Reddit 也非常反对人工智能。但我认为大多数人，或者至少是大多数人，对于这种情况不会消失的事实要么是顺从，要么是兴奋。这就是我们正在寻找的观众。
我们并不是想告诉你人工智能是多么神奇，我们将在新机器政权下进入人工智能乌托邦。我们也不会告诉你这些东西是假的，很糟糕，会自行消失，所以我们不需要做任何事情来监管它或担心它。凯西对此的说法是人工智能现实主义。他认为有很大一部分人只是好奇和感兴趣，也许还有点害怕，但他们对恐惧的反应不是试图把头埋在沙子里，而是试图理解这件事。
因此，当我们进行硬分叉时，我们开始感觉到这一点，我们会做一些似乎不符合我们氛围的事情。我们会做一个克劳德代码演练教程，我们只需要花半个小时构建一个网站，然后拍摄自己的视频，然后把它扔出去，效果会很棒。所以人们显然很好奇，即使视频上的评论都是来自讨厌人工智能的人，但显然对那些“我有点想知道发生了什么”的人有很多需求。
由于多种原因，“我讨厌我无法停止观看这个”是人工智能报道中的一个真正主题。
我们来谈谈这本书吧。我认为这将解答我的许多其他问题。这本书的报道很细致。读起来真的很有趣。正如我听到你描述的那样，它的重点是讲述深度学习革命的历史，因为所有这些人都只是在 Signal 和极其幼稚的推文中谈论。
告诉我这个差距，因为这个行业痴迷于为计算机记录自己，并且对计算机来说是可读的，而对其他人来说却根本不可读，这对我来说似乎很疯狂。所以请解释一下这本书的报道，因为感觉说服他们告诉你发生了什么是一件很困难的事情。
是的，是的。所以基本上我写这篇文章的原因是因为我害怕所有这些东西都会消失。我是一个历史爱好者。我喜欢阅读有关莱特兄弟、美国农村电气化或个人电脑革命期间伟大发明时刻的书籍。我对那些东西很着迷。
当你阅读更多这些书时，你会注意到，它们都依赖于大量同时代的笔记和证据——开发原子弹的科学家的实验室笔记、莱特兄弟与他们的朋友和商业伙伴之间的通信——这些都被保存和存档。
对我来说，每天报道人工智能的时候很清楚，这个东西不会有任何类似的东西，因为所有构建这个东西的人都为私营公司工作。他们不是法律要求保存信件的政府雇员。 B、Signal消息和Slack消息都被律师设置为在一段时间后自动删除。因此，我认为，这些具有历史意义的文物、时刻和故事每年都会大规模消失。
然后C，研究人员都太忙了，没有时间做笔记。他们都在努力，因为他们正在努力打造机器之神。所以，我作为一名记者思考，但更几乎作为一名历史学家，这不是我正式扮演过的角色，但我认为我在这本书中扮演了一个角色。我当时想，“我必须得到这些东西，因为我有这种特权的场边座位。这些人跟我说话。我知道他们中的一些人会坐下来跟我说话，给我讲故事。”
我们在后台做了很多这样的事情，这样他们就可以免受与我交谈的后果的影响。但这是我试图疯狂地获取所有内容并将其放入档案中以供后代可以查看的尝试。
当我读这本书时，真正让我印象深刻的主题是，有那么一刻，AGI 从一个他们都梦想的东西变成了一个他们都必须建造的东西，枷锁脱落了，他们说，“我们必须这样做”，他们都尽其所能地朝着这个目标努力。
你特别谈到了奥弗顿窗口移动的谷歌，突然谷歌内部的人开始谈论通用人工智能，他们认为这只是一个白日梦，而且很愚蠢。那一刻感觉就像人工智能历史上最重要的时刻，“这不是很棒吗？”转到“我们最好尽可能快地走。”
稍微谈谈这一点，因为这些公司内部的转变感觉没有得到充分报道。
是的，我认为这是完全正确的。我的意思是，人们一直在谈论和撰写 AGI 或一些不被称为 AGI 但自古以来含义相同的先驱。尤其是自 20 世纪 50 年代人工智能一词诞生以来，人们就一直在谈论它。艾伦·图灵正在写一篇关于思维机器的文章，它可以做人类大脑能做的任何事情。
所以这个概念已经存在很长时间了，但是市场上或研究实验室中没有任何技术可以真正做到人们想要它做的事情——可以接收信息，学会了解这些信息，然后用它来做出预测并在世界上采取行动。人们尝试了很多不同的方法来做到这一点，但没有一种方法效果很好。
真正需要发生的是变压器的出现。谷歌于 2017 年开发了这个架构，发布后向 OpenAI 等地方展示，OpenAI 采用了 Transformer 的想法并运行它。这就是今天 ChatGPT 中的 T。但那是——
某个谷歌公关人员刚刚从灌木丛中跳出来递给你一张支票。
他们确实喜欢这条线。
当你这么说时，他们就会喜欢。他们变得如此幸福。
他们喜欢它。当你指出虽然他们发明了它，但在 OpenAI 之前他们绝对没能把它变成一个产品时，他们就不那么喜欢它了。
但是，是的，这是一个梦，但没有任何东西可以附加到梦上。没有技术。然后大型语言模型出现了，突然间，“哦，也许这就是可以永远扩展并不断改进多个数量级的东西。”所以，这就是 OpenAI 的灵光一闪，后来在谷歌的灵光乍现，“现在我们有了工具可以做我们一直想做的事情。”
你在那里有一行，你只是指出下一个令牌预测还没有失败——它正在做人们希望它做的所有事情。显然我们必须围绕它开发大量技术。有一些工具可以让代理工作。有强化学习。周围都是这些东西。但该核心技术已经规模化。
我提出这个问题的原因是，从 2023 年到 2024 年，我会询问每一位参加节目或在 The Verge 上看到的人工智能人士，法学硕士是否可以做到这一点。他们能做你想让他们做的事吗？因为我认为当时还不清楚他们可以。
我们现在更近了。他们都在公开谈论 AGI。我们看到 Meta 的 Muse 只要它愿意，就可以在互联网上走来走去。你认为LLM可以做到吗？你认为他们能到达那里吗？

我认为他们可以。我对此并不确定，但到目前为止，它们的效果非常好且有效。如果你回头看看第一个法学硕士，你会发现 99% 的人都认为这很疯狂，而且无法规模化。然后它就在每个阶段、每个数量级上继续工作。我问过人们，下一个令牌预测明显优于之前的所有预测的是什么？有人告诉我这实际上也存在于人脑中。有一个完整的思想流派认为，人脑内部发生的事情本质上是大规模的下一个代币预测。显然，情况要复杂得多。这些并不是彼此的一对一复制品。
但我认为这是人工智能核心的根本谜团：为什么下一个代币预测如此有效？我想我们不知道。我认为这是宇宙奥秘之一，但所有这些之所以有效，是因为下一个令牌的预测结果真的非常非常好地概括。
所有这些公司都必须相信其中的一部分。 Anthropic 的 Dario Amodei 显然写了他的论文《Big Blob of Compute》，他在论文中说你可以做到。您只需转储数据并进行计算即可，我们就会到达那里。其他人都必须相信这一点。
人工智能公司都采取了什么途径才相信这一点，现在他们都完全相信这一点了吗？
我认为他们现在还没有完全相信这一点。我认为他们在不同程度上对此深信不疑。 Ilya Sutskever 有这样一句话：“感受 AGI”，在过去，他会在 OpenAI 的各个楼层中高喊这句话，提醒人们感受 AGI。我认为实验室在不同程度上感受到了通用人工智能。我认为 Anthropic 显然是 AGI 最多的实验室，OpenAI 紧随其后。
然后是谷歌，我认为它一直在努力感受 AGI。我认为这有很多原因，但很有趣。我喜欢这本书的这一部分，其中有谷歌的内部备忘录之争，他们只是在内部留言板上写下这些宣言，然后狙击彼此的宣言之类的东西。

fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Gemini is getting increasingly good at offering personalized information, and its memory plays a huge part in making that possible. The AI tool learns your preferences over time, but you also have the option to explicitly ask it to remember specific things for future reference. We’ve previously spotted Google working on making the process of asking Gemini to remember things easier, and it looks like the tech giant is now focusing on what happens afterward.
As of right now, the easiest way to check everything you’ve explicitly asked Gemini to remember is to ask the AI assistant directly. That could soon change.

You’re reading an Authority Insights story. Authority Insights brings you all the latest exclusive reports, app teardowns, leaks, and in-depth tech coverage from the Android Authority team that you won’t find anywhere else.

Version 17.70.10.sa.arm64 of the Google app gives us our first look at Gemini’s new Remembered items option within the Personal Intelligence section. This is where you’ll be able to “view and manage the text and images you’ve saved to memory,” according to the feature’s description.

Note that the functionality will share this settings menu with Gemini’s existing Memory feature. While Memory tracks things Gemini learns about you from past chats, the new Remembered items section will explicitly track what you’ve told Gemini to remember about you.

As seen in the images above, if and when available, tapping Remembered items will take you to a distinct chat-like interface. The underlying functionality isn’t active yet, and hence the section appears blank with an error at the bottom. When available, this screen should highlight everything Gemini remembers about you.
There also appears to be a text box that could let you add or remove details. Sending instructions through the box also currently highlights an error.
Nevertheless, this is an interesting development that points to Google working toward a more complete Personal Intelligence experience for Gemini users.
This comes soon after we spotted Google working on a dedicated Remember shortcut for the Gemini overlay.

Switching from an iPhone to an Android or vice versa is not the headache it once was. That goes for both the learning curves, or lack thereof, between the platforms, and the tools that now exist that easily port over all of your information. But that doesn’t mean that old rivalries aren’t still at play. Recently, Android Authority’s Harish Jonnalagadda spent three weeks with the iPhone 18 Pro Max and came away with a fairly positive opinion. We put a poll for you, our readers, in the story asking if you would consider switching to iOS at some point, and the reaction was strong.

It shouldn’t be much of a surprise that the majority of people who are on an Android-focused site want only Android devices in their pockets. Out of the 1,265 respondents, 52.8% declared themselves “Android for life.”

cards.title: The RealReal won’t let AI agents hog designer clothing
cards.title_cn: The RealReal 不会让人工智能代理霸占名牌服装
cards.summary: 【The Verge】The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it's updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site. The change comes days after T…
fulltext: Previous reporting by The Verge found that Meta’s Muse could be used to effectively block other shoppers from purchasing items for hours.﻿
The RealReal, a secondhand luxury fashion consignment retailer, said it’s updating its bot defense system, effectively making it harder for AI agents to shop on its site.

The change comes days after The Verge reported that an AI agent could be used to take advantage of The RealReal’s item reserve system. On the retailer’s website, an item goes “on hold” and is unavailable for other customers to buy for 20 minutes once it’s placed in a user’s shopping cart. Using Meta’s Muse, The Verge was able to instruct the AI agent to continuously re-add The RealReal listings in a shopping cart as soon as the 20-minute hold had expired, effectively blocking other shoppers from purchasing products for hours or longer.

After publication, chief technology officer Luke Friang said in an email that the company had addressed the Muse use case flagged by The Verge’s story. The RealReal’s bot defense configuration now makes it much more difficult for all agents to log in, add items to cart, and check out, Friang said. Agents will still be able to surface listings from The RealReal and direct Muse users to product pages, Friang said, adding that the company will continue to strengthen protections as AI-powered online shopping evolves.
Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Technology companies are selling agents as personalized assistants for billions of people — always-on, compliant entities that will schedule meetings, throw parties, and purchase things for human users. So far, agents and shopping seem to go hand in hand; Meta said in its Q3 earnings call this month that it was the most common use case for Muse so far, and that purchases were over $200 on average. Muse has been a hit for Meta and could signal a turning point for AI agents: The company said 10 million people in the US had downloaded the app in 40 days.

But robots shopping for things instead of humans has the potential to upend the balance of the web as we know it. For one, if humans stop visiting websites directly and instead access the web through chatbots, businesses become one step removed from their customers. Retailers — most notably Amazon — have recognized that reality could disrupt their bottom line, especially advertising revenue, and have blocked agents from shopping on their sites.

An influx of AI agents accessing consumer platforms could also break or complicate even the most unexpected things shoppers take for granted, like the reserve system of a used clothing website. There is, of course, a realistic limit to how long a person is willing to spend adding and re-adding designer clothing to their shopping cart if they’re indecisive. An agent in contrast does not care. It is perhaps precisely the type of busywork a fashion-forward person might pay an actual personal assistant to do on their behalf. Now, a capability like this is at the fingertips of millions of consumers, and they are just beginning to learn how to take advantage of it. Retailers, too, are playing catch-up.

fulltext_cn: The Verge 之前的报道发现，Meta 的 Muse 可用于有效阻止其他购物者在数小时内购买商品。
二手奢侈品时尚寄售零售商 The RealReal 表示，它正在更新其机器人防御系统，这实际上使人工智能代理更难在其网站上购物。

这一变化是在 The Verge 报道人工智能代理可用于利用 The RealReal 的物品储备系统几天后发生的。在零售商的网站上，商品一旦放入用户的购物车，就会“暂停”，其他顾客在 20 分钟内无法购买。使用 Meta 的 Muse，The Verge 能够指示 AI 代理在 20 分钟保留期满后不断地将 The RealReal 商品重新添加到购物车中，从而有效地阻止其他购物者在数小时或更长时间内购买产品。

文章发表后，首席技术官 Luke Friang 在一封电子邮件中表示，该公司已经解决了 The Verge 报道中标记的 Muse 用例。 Friang 说，RealReal 的机器人防御配置现在使所有代理登录、将商品添加到购物车和结账变得更加困难。 Friang 表示，代理商仍将能够显示 The RealReal 的列表，并将 Muse 用户引导至产品页面，并补充说，随着人工智能在线购物的发展，该公司将继续加强保护。
Meta 没有立即回应置评请求。

科技公司正在将代理作为数十亿人的个性化助理出售——这些永远在线、合规的实体将为人类用户安排会议、举办派对和购买东西。到目前为止，代理和购物似乎是齐头并进的。 Meta 在本月的第三季度财报电话会议上表示，这是 Muse 迄今为止最常见的用例，平均购买量超过 200 美元。 Muse 对 Meta 来说很受欢迎，可能标志着人工智能代理的转折点：该公司表示，40 天内美国有 1000 万人下载了该应用程序。
但正如我们所知，机器人代替人类购物有可能颠覆网络的平衡。其一，如果人类停止直接访问网站，而是通过聊天机器人访问网络，企业就会远离客户一步。零售商——尤其是亚马逊——已经认识到现实可能会破坏他们的利润，尤其是广告收入，并阻止代理商在其网站上购物。

大量人工智能代理访问消费者平台也可能会破坏购物者认为理所当然的最意想不到的事情或使其复杂化，例如二手服装网站的储备系统。当然，如果一个人犹豫不决，愿意花多长时间在购物车中添加和重新添加名牌服装，那么他们愿意花多长时间当然是有现实限制的。相比之下，代理人并不关心。这也许正是时尚前卫人士可能会花钱请私人助理代为完成的忙碌工作。现在，这样的功能已触手可及，数百万消费者也刚刚开始学习如何利用它。零售商也在奋起直追。

cards.title: I thought I’d love the $180 Fitbit Edge. 7 days later, I’m just disappointed.
cards.title_cn: 我想我会喜欢 180 美元的 Fitbit Edge。 7天后，我很失望。
cards.summary: 【Android Authority】Over the last few months, my priorities in wearables have changed. I’ve realized I don’t care about having Gemini on my wrist, multiple ways to reply to notifications, or even a robust app ecosystem.…
fulltext: Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.

Over the last few months, my priorities in wearables have changed. I’ve realized I don’t care about having Gemini on my wrist, multiple ways to reply to notifications, or even a robust app ecosystem. I simply want a wearable that’s comfortable on my wrist, lasts multiple days on a single charge, and offers a health/fitness tracking suite I enjoy using.

As such, I was really looking forward to the Fitbit Edge. Taking the week-long battery life of the excellent Fitbit Air and giving it a proper touchscreen — all while retaining a small and lightweight design — sounded like the perfect combination. And in some ways, it is.

But after living with the Fitbit Edge for a little over a week, I can’t help but feel disappointed. There’s a lot Google got right here, but between a shocking number of missing features and a lackluster fitness tracking experience, the Fitbit Edge has proven to be a trickier recommendation than I had hoped.

One of the best things about the Fitbit Air is how supremely comfortable it is. You’d think that magic would be lost on the Fitbit Edge due to its display, but the knock-off effect is shockingly minimal.

While the Edge is technically heavier and takes up more space on the wrist, it’s still an extremely svelte piece of hardware. I barely realize I’m wearing it most of the time, and it slides under long sleeves without a problem. It’s honestly kind of amazing just how compact the Edge looks and feels.
But what about the elephant in the room? What about the display? It’s good!

The Fitbit Edge has a 1.3-inch AMOLED panel with always-on display support and Gorilla Glass 3 protection. It’s not a screen that’s going to set the world on fire, but it gets the job done. I haven’t had any issues reading the display on multiple outdoor walks/runs during a very sunny Michigan October, and the touchscreen responsiveness is excellent, too. I do wish there were an automatic brightness sensor, but even without one, the Edge’s display has served me well.

Battery life has also been extremely good. Google promises up to seven days of use per charge, and that promise is right on the money. I got to the end of day seven with a little over 10% battery remaining, and that included six tracked workouts, more auto-detected workouts, and wearing the Edge to bed every night for sleep tracking. I also really appreciate that the charger is the same one used for the Fitbit Air, and that the Edge’s battery is fully user-replaceable. Good job, Google.
Having said all of that, I’m not totally thrilled with some of the smaller hardware details.

On the right side of the Edge’s body is the one and only button. I certainly prefer my wearables with more physical controls, but there’s just not that kind of room on a body this small. It is a good button, but that means most of your interactions happen with the touchscreen — something that’s not always ideal during workouts.
I also don’t love that the Edge introduces yet another proprietary watch band system, and it’s one I’ve not been particularly impressed with.

Google sent me a few different colors of the standard “active band” — black and olive — to accompany the fog color that came with my review unit. The black band picks up oil and hair like you wouldn’t believe, while the olive band has to be jammed into my Fitbit Edge to attach properly, almost as if something’s slightly off with its connector.

This is pretty disappointing for watch bands that start at $40 and go all the way up to $160 (!!) if you splurge on the metal link version. I suspect we’ll see more affordable third-party options over time, but don’t expect a ton to choose from right away.

It’s one thing for the Fitbit Edge to have solid display hardware, but what about the software? You may enjoy looking at the screen, but will you enjoy interacting with the OS it showcases? For the most part, I think you will.

The Fitbit Edge doesn’t run Wear OS (it has its own custom operating system instead), but it shares a lot in common with Google’s smartwatch platform. Swiping left and right on the watch face shows your customizable tiles, swiping down reveals your quick settings, swiping up shows your notifications, and pressing the side button opens your apps menu. If you’ve used Wear OS within the last couple of years, you’ll be right at home.

Whether it’s starting workouts, scrolling through my tiles, or clearing notifications, the Fitbit Edge has felt perfectly fast and responsive. It also looks good, drawing some UI inspiration from Material 3 Expressive. However, while the Edge handles these things extremely well, it also lacks many fundamental “smart” features.

As you’ve probably heard by now, there’s no NFC chip, which means no Google Wallet support for paying with your wrist. For context, this was a core feature of the Fitbit Charge 6 when it launched three years ago. There’s also no microphone or speaker, meaning you can’t reply to texts with your voice, accept phone calls on the Edge, or get audible alarms or workout alerts.

Those are perhaps the biggest omissions, but I’ve also been annoyed by some smaller details, too. There’s no calendar app on the Fitbit Edge. You can’t customize watch faces or tiles on the Edge itself; you have to use the Google Health app for that, and it’s surprisingly clunky to do so.

Most settings (such as AOD and accessibility options) also can’t be accessed from the Edge. You can’t assign custom actions/shortcuts to the physical button, and you can’t customize the workout list in the Exercise app at all — which often results in a lot of scrolling to find the workout type you’re looking for.

I didn’t go into the Fitbit Edge expecting a fully-fledged smartwatch experience, and you shouldn’t either. But the things I’m describing aren’t exclusive to high-end smartwatches — they should be table stakes for just about any fitness tracker, especially one that costs almost $200. Some of these things could be corrected with software updates, but the experience right now is pretty lacking.
When it comes to health and fitness tracking, the Fitbit Edge is considerably more feature-rich. I suppose that’s to be expected, but it’s still good to see how much Google crammed in.

All of the usual suspects are here: step and calorie tracking, sleep tracking, all-day heart rate monitoring and heart rate variability, SpO2 tracking, a skin temperature sensor, and an ECG app. There’s even an altimeter so you can track the floors you climb throughout the day (something the Charge 6 lacked), plus IP68 and 5ATM waterproofing.

Casual, day-to-day health tracking with the Fitbit Edge is solid. Heart-rate accuracy appears to be right on point; the Edge is extremely comfortable to wear in bed for sleep tracking, and it automatically detects multiple workouts without a hitch. If you’re buying the Edge to slap on your wrist to keep an eye on your health in the background, it excels.
Unfortunately, if you’re even slightly serious about manual exercise tracking, this is where the Edge has left me pretty unsatisfied.

My two primary workouts are running and strength training, and neither one is particularly enjoyable on the Fitbit Edge. On the surface, run tracking should be great — there’s built-in GPS, custom goals based on distance, time, or energy burned, and targets you can set for either your pace or HR zone. These things are all great, but once you start running with the Fitbit Edge, you realize how limiting the rest of the experience really is.

There are no vibration alerts to speak of; not for mile splits or goal progress. I set a 6.22-mile goal for one of my runs, and I had to keep checking the Edge to see how much progress I was making because the tracker just doesn’t send those alerts. You also can’t customize the workout screens. Since there’s no default screen that shows heart rate zones and your pace on a single page, I had to scroll back and forth between them throughout the entire run.

Adding on top of that, GPS accuracy just isn’t very good. On that 6.22-mile run, the Fitbit Edge tracked 6.25 miles, whereas Strava and my Amazfit watch tracked 6.42 miles. Having run that same route multiple times over the years, I also know just from my personal experience that the Edge was undercounting.

What’s the issue with strength training? The Edge doesn’t support tracking individual sets, reps, and weights, which means missing out on a lot of valuable data. The Pixel Watch 5 will support this more detailed tracking at some point in the future, but there’s no word from Google on whether it’ll ever come to the Fitbit Edge. Given there’s no technical limitation preventing this, it’s rather frustrating.

I suppose I should also talk about Google Health. Just like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, this is where all your health data from the Fitbit Edge is stored. I was pretty disappointed with Google Health when I used it earlier this summer, and I was curious to see how it had changed a few months following its big launch.

While Google Health is far from perfect, I’m happy to report that it is noticeably better today than it used to be. The “expanded view” for your focus tabs is a great touch, and customizing these tabs is easier, too. AI summaries for workouts, sleep tracking, and other health updates are much less wordy, and I appreciate that you can turn these off entirely if you prefer. Google has also squashed some of the most annoying bugs, such as missing or slow-loading maps from outdoor workouts.

I still wish Google would find a better way to present health data on the Today page that’s less centered on AI blurbs, and interacting with the Health Coach remains hit-or-miss (though it is more reliable than it once was). But those critiques aside, I have to admit that I’ve enjoyed using Google Health more than I expected.

I simply want a wearable that’s comfortable on my wrist, lasts multiple days on a single charge, and offers a health/fitness tracking suite I enjoy using. That’s what I said at the top of this review, and the Fitbit Edge comes so close to meeting all of those things. But in its current state, it’s simply too undercooked and missing too many features for me to keep wearing it as my wearable of choice.

Not having a calendar app on the Edge or restricting so many settings to the Google Health companion app are annoying, but I’d be willing to overlook those things if Google really nailed the health/fitness experience. But the fact is that it didn’t. While many parts of it are very good, not supporting basic workout progress alerts or customizable exercise screens — paired with pretty lackluster GPS accuracy — throws that argument out the window.

I get that some people may point out that the Fitbit Edge is “only” $180, and therefore I should set my expectations in check. But compared to what else is out there, I’d argue that the Fitbit Edge is fairly overpriced for what it actually offers.

The Samsung Galaxy Fit 3 can be purchased for less than $60 at the time of writing, and it offers a similarly robust health tracking experience in a compact body, with even longer battery life and a much larger screen. There’s no built-in GPS, but considering how bad the Edge’s GPS performance is, I don’t think that’s a huge loss. And if you don’t mind stepping up to a more traditional smartwatch design, the Amazfit Active 3 offers significantly more robust workout tracking (especially with running and strength training), built-in GPS, four physical buttons, a microphone and speaker, plus a 1.32-inch AMOLED screen with sapphire glass — all for just $170.

The only real reason to buy the Fitbit Edge over one of these competing wearables is if you’re committed to using Google Health. But even then, I’m not sure buying the Fitbit Edge instead of the Fitbit Air ($99 at Amazon) or a Pixel Watch is the right move.

If you just want something for casual health tracking, the Fitbit Air feels like the better choice. It’s substantially cheaper, offers health features extremely similar to the Edge’s, and the simplicity of its screenless design comes with its own benefits. Pixel Watches are expensive, but if you can find a good deal on a Pixel Watch 5 ($399 at Amazon) or Pixel Watch 4 ($349.99 at Amazon) — which should be easy during the holiday shopping season — the benefits are tremendous, both in smart features and workout tracking.

In my initial hands-on with the Fitbit Edge, I said I thought Google might have found the sweet spot with its latest wearable. But having now actually used and lived with it, I think it’s more accurate to say that the Fitbit Edge feels stuck in the middle.

It’s certainly not the worst wearable you can buy, but whether you’re looking at alternatives from different brands or from Google itself, the Fitbit Edge doesn’t make a strong enough case for choosing it over those other options.

2026 年 10 月 26 日 — 东部时间下午 1:00
在过去的几个月里，我对可穿戴设备的优先考虑发生了变化。我意识到我并不关心手腕上有 Gemini、回复通知的多种方式，甚至是强大的应用程序生态系统。我只是想要一款佩戴在手腕上舒适、一次充电可持续使用多天、并且提供我喜欢使用的健康/健身追踪套件的可穿戴设备。
因此，我真的很期待 Fitbit Edge。采用出色的 Fitbit Air 长达一周的电池续航时间，并为其配备合适的触摸屏，同时保留小巧轻便的设计，听起来像是完美的组合。从某些方面来说，确实如此。
但在使用 Fitbit Edge 一个多星期后，我不禁感到失望。谷歌在这里提供了很多东西，但在数量惊人的缺失功能和乏善可陈的健身追踪体验之间，Fitbit Edge 已被证明是一个比我希望的更棘手的推荐。
Fitbit Air 的一大优点就是它非常舒适。你可能会认为 Fitbit Edge 的魔力会因为它的显示屏而消失，但仿冒效果却微乎其微。
虽然 Edge 从技术上来说更重并且占用了更多的手腕空间，但它仍然是一款极其纤薄的硬件。我几乎没有意识到我大部分时间都戴着它，而且它可以毫无问题地滑到长袖下面。老实说，Edge 的外观和感觉如此紧凑，真是令人惊叹。
但是房间里的大象呢？显示器怎么样？很好！
Fitbit Edge 配备 1.3 英寸 AMOLED 面板，支持常亮显示和 Gorilla Glass 3 保护。这不是一个会点燃世界的屏幕，但它可以完成任务。在阳光明媚的密歇根十月，我在多次户外散步/跑步时阅读显示屏时没有遇到任何问题，而且触摸屏的响应能力也非常出色。我确实希望有一个自动亮度传感器，但即使没有，Edge 的显示屏也对我很有帮助。
电池寿命也非常好。谷歌承诺每次充电最多可使用 7 天，这一承诺是物有所值的。到第七天结束时，我的电池电量还剩 10% 多一点，其中包括六次跟踪锻炼、更多自动检测锻炼以及每晚佩戴 Edge 睡觉进行睡眠跟踪。我还非常欣赏 Fitbit Air 所使用的充电器与 Edge 的电池完全可由用户更换。干得好，谷歌。
说了这么多，我对一些较小的硬件细节并不完全感到兴奋。
Edge 机身右侧是唯一的按钮。我当然更喜欢具有更多物理控制功能的可穿戴设备，但这么小的机身上没有这样的空间。这是一个很好的按钮，但这意味着您的大部分交互都是通过触摸屏进行的 - 这在锻炼期间并不总是理想的。
我也不喜欢 Edge 引入了另一种专有的表带系统，而且我对此并没有特别印象深刻。
谷歌给我发送了几种不同颜色的标准“活动带”——黑色和橄榄色——来搭配我的评测设备附带的雾色。黑色表带会沾上油脂和头发，你简直不敢相信，而橄榄色表带则必须卡入我的 Fitbit Edge 才能正确连接，几乎就像连接器有什么问题一样。
对于起价 40 美元，一直到 160 美元（！！）的表带来说，如果你花大价钱购买金属链节版本，这真是令人失望。我怀疑随着时间的推移，我们会看到更多实惠的第三方选择，但不要指望立即有大量选择。
Fitbit Edge 拥有坚固的显示硬件是一回事，但软件呢？您可能喜欢看屏幕，但您会喜欢与它展示的操作系统交互吗？在大多数情况下，我想你会的。
Fitbit Edge 不运行 Wear OS（它有自己的定制操作系统），但它与谷歌的智能手表平台有很多共同点。在表盘上左右滑动可显示可自定义的图块，向下滑动可显示快速设置，向上滑动可显示通知，按侧面按钮可打开应用程序菜单。如果您在过去几年中使用过 Wear OS，那么您将会感到宾至如归。
无论是开始锻炼、滚动浏览图块还是清除通知，Fitbit Edge 都感觉非常快速且反应灵敏。它看起来也不错，从 Material 3 Expressive 中汲取了一些 UI 灵感。然而，虽然 Edge 能够很好地处理这些事情，但它也缺乏许多基本的“智能”功能。
您现在可能已经听说过，它没有 NFC 芯片，这意味着 Google 钱包不支持手腕支付。就背景而言，这是三年前推出的 Fitbit Charge 6 的核心功能。它还没有麦克风或扬声器，这意味着您无法用语音回复短信、在 Edge 上接听电话、或接收声音警报或锻炼提醒。
这些可能是最大的遗漏，但我也对一些较小的细节感到恼火。 Fitbit Edge 上没有日历应用程序。您无法在 Edge 本身上自定义表盘或图块；你必须使用谷歌健康应用程序才能做到这一点，而且这样做非常笨拙。
大多数设置（例如 AOD 和辅助功能选项）也无法从 Edge 访问。您无法将自定义操作/快捷方式分配给物理按钮，并且根本无法自定义锻炼应用程序中的锻炼列表 - 这通常会导致大量滚动才能找到您正在寻找的锻炼类型。
我并没有期待 Fitbit Edge 能带来成熟的智能手表体验，你也不应该。但我所描述的东西并不是高端智能手表所独有的——它们应该成为几乎所有健身追踪器的赌注，尤其是价格近 200 美元的一款。其中一些问题可以通过软件更新来纠正，但目前的体验非常缺乏。
在健康和健身追踪方面，Fitbit Edge 的功能要丰富得多。我想这是可以预料到的，但看到谷歌的投入还是很高兴的。
所有常见的嫌疑人都在这里：步数和卡路里跟踪、睡眠跟踪、全天心率监测和心率变异性、SpO2 跟踪、皮肤温度传感器和心电图应用程序。甚至还有一个高度计，让您可以追踪全天攀登的楼层（这是 Charge 6 所缺少的），此外还具有 IP68 和 5ATM 防水功能。
Fitbit Edge 的休闲日常健康追踪功能非常可靠。心率准确度似乎很准确； Edge 佩戴在床上进行睡眠追踪非常舒适，并且可以轻松自动检测多种锻炼。如果您购买 Edge 是为了在手腕上拍一下以在后台监视您的健康状况，那么它会非常适合。
不幸的是，如果你对手动运动追踪稍微认真一点，这就是 Edge 让我非常不满意的地方。
我的两项主要锻炼是跑步和力量训练，但在 Fitbit Edge 上，这两项锻炼都不是特别令人愉快。从表面上看，跑步跟踪应该很棒——有内置的 GPS、基于距离、时间或消耗的能量的自定义目标，以及您可以为配速或心率区设置的目标。这些东西都很棒，但一旦您开始使用 Fitbit Edge 跑步，您就会意识到其余体验的限制。
没有振动警报可言；不是为了里程分割或目标进度。我为其中一次跑步设定了 6.22 英里的目标，我必须不断检查 Edge 以了解我取得了多少进展，因为跟踪器不会发送这些警报。您也无法自定义锻炼屏幕。由于没有默认屏幕在单个页面上显示心率区域和配速，因此我必须在整个跑步过程中在它们之间来回滚动。
除此之外，GPS 精度也不是很好。在 6.22 英里的跑步中，Fitbit Edge 追踪了 6.25 英里，而 Strava 和我的 Amazfit 手表追踪了 6.42 英里。多年来，我多次跑过同一条路线，根据我的个人经验，我也知道 Edge 低估了。
力量训练有什么问题？ Edge 不支持跟踪单组、次数和重量，这意味着会错过很多有价值的数据。 Pixel Watch 5 将在未来某个时候支持这种更详细的跟踪功能，但谷歌没有透露它是否会出现在 Fitbit Edge 上。鉴于没有技术限制可以阻止这种情况，这相当令人沮丧。
我想我还应该谈谈 Google Health。就像 Pixel Watch 和 Fitbit Air 一样，Fitbit Edge 上的所有健康数据都存储在此处。今年夏天早些时候使用 Google Health 时，我对它感到非常失望，而且我很好奇它在发布几个月后发生了怎样的变化。
虽然 Google Health 远非完美，但我很高兴地向大家报告，它现在比以前明显更好了。焦点选项卡的“扩展视图”非常棒，而且自定义这些选项卡也更容易。锻炼、睡眠跟踪和其他健康更新的人工智能摘要就不那么啰嗦了，如果你愿意的话，我很感激你可以完全关闭这些。谷歌还解决了一些最烦人的错误，例如户外锻​​炼地图丢失或加载缓慢。
我仍然希望谷歌能找到一种更好的方式在“今日”页面上呈现健康数据，而不是以人工智能简介为中心，并且与健康教练的互动仍然是偶然的（尽管它比以前更可靠）。但抛开这些批评不谈，我不得不承认，我比我想象的更喜欢使用 Google Health。
我只是想要一款佩戴在手腕上舒适、一次充电可持续使用多天、并且提供我喜欢使用的健康/健身追踪套件的可穿戴设备。这就是我在这篇评论的开头所说的，Fitbit Edge 非常接近满足所有这些要求。但在目前的状态下，它还不够成熟，缺少太多功能，我无法继续将它作为我的可穿戴设备选择。
Edge 上没有日历应用程序或限制 Google Health 配套应用程序的如此多设置很烦人，但如果 Google 真的能提供健康/健身体验，我愿意忽略这些事情。但事实并非如此。虽然它的许多部分都非常好，但不支持基本的锻炼进度警报或可定制的锻炼屏幕——再加上相当乏善可陈的 GPS 精度——让这一论点被抛到了九霄云外。
我知道有些人可能会指出 Fitbit Edge“仅”180 美元，因此我应该控制自己的期望。但与其他产品相比，我认为 Fitbit Edge 的实际价格相当高。

截至撰写本文时，三星 Galaxy Fit 3 的售价不到 60 美元，它在紧凑的机身中提供了同样强大的健康跟踪体验，并且具有更长的电池寿命和更大的屏幕。没有内置 GPS，但考虑到 Edge 的 GPS 性能有多糟糕，我认为这并不是一个巨大的损失。如果你不介意采用更传统的智能手表设计，Amazfit Active 3 提供更强大的锻炼追踪功能（尤其是跑步和力量训练）、内置 GPS、四个物理按钮、麦克风和扬声器，以及带有蓝宝石玻璃的 1.32 英寸 AMOLED 屏幕 - 所有这些仅需 170 美元。
购买 Fitbit Edge 而不是这些竞争对手的可穿戴设备的唯一真正原因是，您是否致力于使用 Google Health。但即便如此，我也不确定购买 Fitbit Edge 而不是 Fitbit Air（亚马逊售价 99 美元）或 Pixel Watch 是否正确。

如果您只想进行休闲健康追踪，Fitbit Air 感觉是更好的选择。它的价格便宜得多，提供与 Edge 极其相似的健康功能，而且其无屏幕设计的简单性也有其自身的好处。 Pixel Watch 价格昂贵，但如果你能找到划算的 Pixel Watch 5（亚马逊 399 美元）或 Pixel Watch 4（亚马逊 349.99 美元）——这在假日购物季应该很容易——那么好处是巨大的，无论是在智能功能还是锻炼跟踪方面。
在我最初试用 Fitbit Edge 时，我说我认为谷歌可能已经找到了其最新可穿戴设备的最佳位置。但现在实际使用并与之相处后，我认为更准确的说法是 Fitbit Edge 感觉卡在中间。
它当然不是你能买到的最差的可穿戴设备，但无论你是在寻找不同品牌的替代品还是谷歌本身的替代品，Fitbit Edge 都没有足够的理由让你选择它而不是其他选择。

SpaceX has reached a binding commitment for roughly $40 billion in financing for AI chips and related data center equipment, the company disclosed in a regulatory filing Monday. In a statement, SpaceX called the deal the “largest committed GPU financing”.

Under the agreement, an entity managed by Apollo Global Management, the New York-based private equity giant, will buy the chips and related server hardware, then lease the equipment to SpaceX. The leases will last about five to five-and-a-quarter years, beginning when each tranche of equipment is delivered, according to the filing.
SpaceX expects the deal to close by year-end, subject to closing conditions, with leases starting in the first half of 2027 as the GPUs and related equipment arrive.
The financing gives SpaceX another way to fund its rapidly expanding AI ambitions without relying solely on traditional debt markets.

“This lease diversifies our funding sources and addresses a notable portion of the funding required to deliver on our growth plans,” SpaceX CFO Bret Johnsen said in a statement Monday, noting it is seeing “less than one-year payback periods” on its AI infrastructure investments as it scales compute to power Grok and its cloud services.
Apollo said the financing will help deliver Nvidia’s next-generation Vera Rubin chips for SpaceX’s “terrestrial compute buildout.”
The financing comes as SpaceX ramps spending to expand its AI infrastructure, alongside its Starlink and launch businesses.

The financing follows a blockbuster third quarter for SpaceX’s AI business. SpaceX’s AI segment, which includes the Grok chatbot, the Cursor coding tool, and its cloud compute business, outperformed investor expectations in the third quarter and brought in $7.6 billion of SpaceX’s $14.6 billion in revenue, more than Starlink and rocket launches combined.

Capital expenditures also surged to nearly $20 billion, up from $6.9 billion a year earlier, as SpaceX races to expand its compute footprint. CFO Bret Johnsen said on the company’s October 20 earnings call that SpaceX expects to spend $35 billion to $40 billion in the fourth quarter alone.
The massive lease comes after a tumultuous stretch in the debt markets for AI infrastructure players, as investors grow squeamish over runaway capital expenditures and limited profits.
While SpaceX had no trouble tapping Wall Street, Musk used the $40 billion announcement to take a victory lap over pure-play AI compute rivals.

Pointing to SpaceX’s “investment-grade” status and steady cash flow from Starlink and rocket launches, Musk argued on Sunday that debt markets have largely closed the door on companies without major revenue streams outside of AI data centers — spelling trouble for the more than 200 neocloud companies built solely to rent out GPUs for AI workloads.
“That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation,” Musk wrote on X. “Some will make it through, but not many.”

SpaceX 周一在一份监管​​文件中披露，该公司已达成具有约束力的承诺，为人工智能芯片和相关数据中心设备提供约 400 亿美元的融资。 SpaceX 在一份声明中称这笔交易是“最大的 GPU 承诺融资”。
根据协议，总部位于纽约的私募股权巨头 Apollo Global Management 管理的实体将购买芯片和相关服务器硬件，然后将设备租赁给 SpaceX。文件称，租赁期将持续约五到五年又四分之一年，从每批设备交付时开始。
SpaceX 预计该交易将在年底前完成，但须符合成交条件，随着 GPU 和相关设备抵达，租赁将于 2027 年上半年开始。
此次融资为 SpaceX 提供了另一种方式来为其快速扩张的人工智能雄心提供资金，而无需仅仅依赖传统的债务市场。
SpaceX 首席财务官布雷特·约翰森 (Bret Johnsen) 在周一的一份声明中表示：“这项租赁使我们的资金来源多样化，并解决了实现我们增长计划所需的大部分资金。”他指出，随着公司扩展计算以支持 Grok 及其云服务，其人工智能基础设施投资的“投资回收期不到一年”。
Apollo 表示，这笔融资将有助于为 SpaceX 的“地面计算扩建”提供 Nvidia 的下一代 Vera Rubin 芯片。
此次融资正值 SpaceX 加大支出以扩大其人工智能基础设施以及星链和发射业务之际。
此次融资是在 SpaceX 的人工智能业务第三季度取得轰动效应之后进行的。 SpaceX 的人工智能部门，包括 Grok 聊天机器人、Cursor 编码工具及其云计算业务，第三季度的表现超出了投资者的预期，为 SpaceX 146 亿美元的收入带来了 76 亿美元的收入，超过了 Starlink 和火箭发射的总和。
随着 SpaceX 竞相扩大其计算足迹，资本支出也从一年前的 69 亿美元飙升至近 200 亿美元。首席财务官 Bret Johnsen 在公司 10 月 20 日的财报电话会议上表示，SpaceX 预计仅第四季度就将支出 350 亿至 400 亿美元。
此次大规模租赁是在人工智能基础设施参与者的债务市场经历了一段动荡之后发生的，因为投资者对失控的资本支出和有限的利润感到不安。
尽管 SpaceX 在与华尔街的接触中没有遇到任何困难，但马斯克利用 400 亿美元的宣布，战胜了纯粹的人工智能计算竞争对手。
周日，马斯克在谈到 SpaceX 的“投资级”地位以及来自 Starlink 和火箭发射的稳定现金流时表示，债务市场基本上已经对在 AI 数据中心之外没有主要收入来源的公司关闭了大门，这给 200 多家专为出租 GPU 用于 AI 工作负载而建立的 Neocloud 公司带来了麻烦。
“这意味着 200 多个新云将出现孔雀鱼级别的死亡和整合，”马斯克在 X 上写道，“有些会挺过去，但不多。”

cards.title: Our newest AI Quest: Mapping the human brain
cards.title_cn: 我们最新的人工智能任务：绘制人类大脑图谱
cards.summary: 【Google】Learn AI literacy via Google’s latest AI Quests lesson on neuroscience, “Polar Peaks.”
fulltext: Today, we’re launching “Polar Peaks”, our third quest in the AI Quests series, created by Google Research and the Stanford Accelerator for Learning to teach students how AI works and how to use it responsibly. AI Quests invites students ages 11 to 14 to step into the shoes of Google researchers to tackle some of humanity’s biggest challenges.
More than 400,000 quests have been completed to date, localized to 10 languages. Alongside the new quest, we’re also releasing training modules for teachers.

In the first two quests, students tackle flood forecasting and eye disease detection, inspired by Google Research’s Flood Forecasting initiative and AI model for diabetic retinopathy screening. Our newest quest, “Polar Peaks,” has students travel to the frontiers of neuroscience and see how AI can speed up scientific research.

With the guidance of in-game mentors, students scan and map the neurons in the brain to better understand the game character’s memory loss. They complete tasks like data cleaning and model testing, learning firsthand that AI requires careful human oversight and critical thinking.

The quest is inspired by over a decade of our research in connectomics: the science of mapping neural networks in the brain. Upon completion of the quest, students hear from two researchers behind our real-world breakthroughs, including the recent mapping of the complete fruit fly brain, the largest brain map by number of neurons to date.

Teachers play a critical role in bringing the quests to life and fitting them into their existing classroom curriculum. We’re rolling out new dedicated teacher training modules to help educators reinforce key AI literacy concepts and use AI Quests for learning and discussion. These are launching within the Google AI Educator Series. The modules for Quest #1 and #2 are accessible here. The training module for Quest #3 will follow next month.

Earlier this year, AI Quests won a 2026 Webby Award for AI Education, Learning & Training, and Best Global K–12 Learning Solution at the ETIH Innovation Awards. We’ll continue working with educators and partners to bring more quests to more classrooms this school year.

cards.summary_cn: 【Google】通过 Google 最新的神经科学 AI Quests 课程“Polar Peaks”学习 AI 素养。
fulltext_cn: 今天，我们将推出人工智能任务系列中的第三个任务“极地峰”，该任务由 Google Research 和斯坦福学习加速器创建，旨在向学生传授人工智能的工作原理以及如何负责任地使用它。 AI Quests 邀请 11 至 14 岁的学生扮演 Google 研究人员的角色，解决人类面临的一些最大挑战。
迄今为止，已完成超过 400,000 个任务，并已本地化为 10 种语言。除了新任务之外，我们还发布了教师培训模块。
在前两个任务中，学生们受 Google 研究的洪水预报计划和糖尿病视网膜病变筛查人工智能模型的启发，解决洪水预报和眼部疾病检测问题。我们最新的任务“极地峰”让学生们前往神经科学的前沿，了解人工智能如何加速科学研究。
在游戏中导师的指导下，学生扫描并绘制大脑中的神经元图，以更好地了解游戏角色的记忆丧失情况。他们完成数据清理和模型测试等任务，亲身了解到人工智能需要仔细的人类监督和批判性思维。
这一探索的灵感来自我们十多年来对连接组学的研究：绘制大脑中神经网络的科学。完成任务后，学生们将听到两位研究人员讲述我们在现实世界中取得的突破，包括最近绘制的完整果蝇大脑图谱，这是迄今为止按神经元数量计算的最大大脑图谱。
教师在将任务变为现实并将其融入现有课堂课程方面发挥着关键作用。我们正在推出新的专用教师培训模块，以帮助教育工作者强化关键的人工智能素养概念，并使用人工智能任务进行学习和讨论。这些都是在 Google AI Educator 系列中推出的。任务 #1 和 #2 的模块可在此处访问。任务 #3 的培训模块将于下个月推出。
今年早些时候，AI Quests 荣获 2026 年人工智能教育、学习和培训威比奖，以及 ETIH 创新奖最佳全球 K-12 学习解决方案。我们将继续与教育工作者和合作伙伴合作，在本学年为更多教室带来更多任务。

fulltext: IT之家 10 月 26 日消息，据浙江高速公路智能收费运营服务有限公司，为贯彻落实交通运输部关于高速公路“手机 +”无卡便捷通行的工作部署，深化技术创新与服务升级，更好地服务人民群众便捷美好出行，浙江省“手机 +”无卡通行业务将于 2026 年 10 月 29 日上午 9 时正式上线。
车主可通过“浙江 ETC 手机 +”微信小程序快速完成车辆认证注册，通行高速时入口无需领卡，系统自动识别抬杆，出口扫码支付后即可驶离。注册用户可在“浙江 ETC 手机 +”微信小程序查询通行记录、开具发票。

IT之家注意到，交通运输部此前印发了《高速公路“手机 +”无卡便捷通行实施方案（2026-2028 年）》，积极稳妥推广“手机 +”无卡便捷通行模式。该模式以手机为载体，主要通过车牌识别技术还原车辆全程行驶轨迹并核算通行费用，用户可通过现行 MTC（人工收费）车道的电子支付方式付款。未安装 ETC 的小型载客汽车使用此模式可以省去传统人工车道领取、交还 CPC 卡的操作流程，实现“免取卡、免还卡”便捷通行。
